title: 印刷工場を買い取る  (Buying the Printing Factory)

segments.t: Fresh from the studio shoot, Muranishi tells Kawada why every project needs a real story, then brings him straight to Yoshikawa's printing factory. When the cautious proprietor refuses to print for them, Kawada and Muranishi offer to buy the entire factory in cash. Listen to the rhythm of the negotiation first.
脳を刺激するストーリーが必要なんですよ。
作りたいものを作りにですよ。
どうしても無理ですかね？
では、この工場を買い取ります。
無理な話だよ。資金が足りないよ。
問屋は？
もちろん挟まない。
一カ月以内に買えますよ。
即金で五千万出しますよ。
ちょっと幹部連中と話してきます。
ずっと待ってました、あなたのような人を。
いけます！
Business numbers and bold promises drive this negotiation at Yoshikawa's factory. Let's break down each turn.
脳を刺激するストーリーが必要なんですよ。
'You need a story that stimulates the mind.' Borrowed English "sutoorii" pairs with "hitsuyou", necessary or needed. Before it, "nou" means brain, and "shigeki suru" means to stimulate or spark.
作りたいものを作りにですよ。
'To go make what we want to make.' Muranishi stacks "tsukuritai mono"—the thing we want to make—before "tsukuri ni", which expresses going somewhere in order to make it.
どうしても無理ですかね？

'Is it really impossible no matter what?' "Doushite mo" adds 'no matter what' or 'by any means', while "muri" is the go-to word for impossible or asking too much. Ending on "desu ka ne" softens the question into a hopeful probe.
では、この工場を買い取ります。
'Then we will buy out this factory.' Formal "dewa" pivots cleanly with 'well then'. "Kono koujou" points to 'this factory', and "kaitorimasu" joins "kau", to buy, with "toru", to take over.
無理な話だよ。資金が足りないよ。

'That is an impossible idea. You do not have enough funds.' Here "muri" returns as "muri na hanashi", an unrealistic proposal. "Shikin" means business funds or capital, and "tarinai" says an amount falls short.
問屋は？
'What about wholesalers?' Two words—"tonya", wholesaler, plus topic marker "wa" with a rising lilt—are all Japanese needs to ask 'and what about the middlemen?'.
もちろん挟まない。

'Of course we leave them out.' "Mochiron" means 'of course' and works all by itself too. "Hasamanai" comes from "hasamu", to sandwich or put in between, meaning they will put nobody between factory and shop.
一カ月以内に買えますよ。
'We can buy it within one month.' "Ikkagetsu" counts a one-month span, followed by "inai ni" for 'within'. "Kaemasu" flips "kau", to buy, into 'can buy'.
即金で五千万出しますよ。

'I will pay fifty million right now in cash.' Japanese groups big numbers by ten-thousands, called "man", so fifty million is "gosenman"—literally five thousand ten-thousands. "Sokkin de" means spot cash on the table, and "dashimasu" promises to put it up.
ちょっと幹部連中と話してきます。
'I will go talk with the executives for a moment.' Joining "hanashite" with "kimasu"—literally 'talk and come back'—is how Japanese says 'I will go talk to them and be right back'.
ずっと待ってました、あなたのような人を。

'I have been waiting all along for someone like you.' "Zutto" stretches time out as 'all along', before "mattemashita", the spoken form of 'was waiting'. "Anata no you na hito" builds 'a person like you' right in front of "hito", person.
いけます！

'This will work!' From everyday "iku", to go, "ikemasu" means 'it can go forward'—a punchy Japanese way to cheer 'this is going to work!'. Now let's hear the whole factory negotiation again from start to finish.
脳を刺激するストーリーが必要なんですよ。
作りたいものを作りにですよ。
どうしても無理ですかね？
では、この工場を買い取ります。
無理な話だよ。資金が足りないよ。
問屋は？
もちろん挟まない。
一カ月以内に買えますよ。
即金で五千万出しますよ。
ちょっと幹部連中と話してきます。
ずっと待ってました、あなたのような人を。
いけます！
Remember "muri" whenever a plan sounds impossible, "mochiron" for an easy 'of course', and "ikemasu" when everything clicks into place. Until next scene.
また会いましょう。
